newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS - Czech Nova Hut steel signs IFC loan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Czech Nova Hut steel signs IFC loan.

text.p: Nova Hut a.s., seen as the most promising part of a struggling Czech steel sector, got a boost on Friday by completing an international debt package to finance its modernisation plans.
The International Finance Corp (IFC), the corporate financing arm of the World Bank, signed a $250 million credit deal with Nova Hut, which is based in the northeastern city of Ostrava.
It is divided into a $75 million, 12-year loan on the IFC's own account, and a $175 million, 10-year senior syndicated loan from 17 international banks.

The loans, which have no government guarantees, are priced well above the Czech National Bank's sovereign benchmark set earlier this month. The central bank was granted a $2 billion syndicated credit line at 10 basis points above the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR).
A senior official involved in arranging the credit told Reuters that the IFC loan was priced at 162.5 basis points above LIBOR, while the syndicated credit was at 137.5 basis points over LIBOR.

The IFC deal also calls for the Czech government to reduce its 67.25 percent stake in Nova Hut to a minority 49 percent within three months. The stake is held by the National Property Fund, the state privatisation agency.
Officials involved in negotiating the loan said Czech reluctance to divest the stake had held up the signing for weeks.

Part of the money is to be used for a hot-rolled coil mini mill built by U.S.-based ICF Kaiser International, which also signed the second $160 million part of a $262 million project to manage the construction of the mill.

The project, worth a total of $650 million, is to be completed by 2000. It should help Nova Hut to compete abroad as a low-cost producer of flat steel rather than its traditional ingot-type long steel products, officials said.

"The IFC financing, the largest ever arranged by the IFC in the Czech Republic, will enable Nova Hut to embark on a comprehensive modernisation and environmental upgrade of its steel complex in Ostrava," an IFC statement said.
Nova Hut has become the most promising steelworks out of a handful of large Czech mills which are trying to slim down and find new markets after years of Communist-era inefficiencies.

The plan calls for Nova Hut to cut its nominal crude steel capacity by one million tonnes to three million a year. It should switch into higher-yielding, more efficient flat steel production, the IFC said.

The largest participant in the syndicate is Germany's Deutsche Bank which contributed $19 million. Eight Japanese banks provided 40 percent of the financing, and the group also included Austrian, South Korean, U.S. and Belgian banks.
Another 2.7 billion crowns ($84 million) will come from a domestic syndicated loan to be arranged in the next three weeks by Prague-based Komercni Banka a.s..
Komercni Banka chief executive Richard Salzmann told Reuters that the domestic syndicate would consist of two or three banks.
The remaining financing for the modernisation would come from Nova Hut's cash flow, IFC officials said.

NPF Chairman Roman Ceska said that the NPF would sell an 18.25 percent stake in Nova Hut to Komercni Banka and Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB). Both are expected to sell the shares to third parties or place them on stock markets.

Salzmann said his bank expected to place the shares it would hold on the Czech stock market. CSFB officials were not immediately available for comment. Salzmann did not specify how many Nova Hut shares Komercni expected to hold.
Nova Hut's net profit dropped 110 million crowns to 254 million in 1996 on turnover of 23.2 billion.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003 ($ = 32.27 Czech Crowns)
